title: The spider's house
hookLine: the frailest of houses is the spider's (29:41)

lines: WALK THROUGH ONE, AND IT'S GONE.
cards: Early morning, after a damp night, they're everywhere: webs strung between fence posts, across window corners, between stems in the garden, each one beaded with dew, catching the light.
They're beautiful, and a spider worked hard on each one. Then you walk through one without seeing it, and it's gone, a few strands on your sleeve.
Surah Al-'Ankabut is named for that web, and for one verse that uses it as a picture.

teach.h: OTHER PATRONS: WHAT YOU LEAN ON.

teach.b: Pickthall: "The likeness of those who choose other patrons than Allah is as the likeness of the spider when she taketh unto herself a house, and lo! the frailest of all houses is the spider's house, if they but knew."
Three things to notice. First, patrons: awliya', protectors, the ones you lean on. The verse is about where people put their weight.
Second, the spider isn't lazy or foolish.

teach.h: SHE BUILDS, AND IT CAN'T HOLD.
teach.b: She builds, and what she builds is intricate and real. As shelter, it just can't hold: it keeps out nothing, not rain, not wind, not a careless hand.
Third, the ending: if they but knew. As if the people leaning on the wrong thing could see it, if they looked.
Before this verse, the surah tells of peoples, Nuh's, Ibrahim's, Lut's, 'Ad, Thamud, Qarun, Pharaoh, who trusted in their strength, their wealth, their idols, and found it was thread.

teach.h: THE WEB AT THE CAVE: A STORY TOLD.
teach.b: There's also a story often told from the Prophet's journey to Medina: when he and Abu Bakr hid in the cave of Thawr, a spider spun a web across the entrance, and the pursuers passed by.
That's a story people tell, and its chains are weak; the Qur'an mentions the cave but not the spider. So the same creature appears in two pictures. In the verse, the web is the frailest of houses.
In the story, a frail web, held by God, protects. What matters, in both, is who you lean on.

how: Muslims read the parable of the spider's house as a reminder to rely on God rather than on idols, wealth or status, and the surah is named Al-'Ankabut for this verse.

o: the cave where the Prophet hid on his journey
a web of lies that traps the one who spins it
the spider, whose house is the frailest of all

games.q: the spider's house — tap the pairs.
p: patrons, protectors, what you lean on

s: the verse calls the spider foolish or lazy
she builds carefully; the point is that the house can't hold.
the Qur'an tells of a spider spinning across the cave of Thawr
the Qur'an mentions the cave; the spider is a story with weak chains.
the surah tells of earlier peoples before this verse
Nuh's, Ibrahim's and Lut's people, 'Ad, Thamud, Qarun and Pharaoh come first.

games.q: you've built something careful and beautiful to lean on: status, savings, people's approval. the wind is rising. what does the verse say?
o: it'll hold if you built it well enough.
the frailest of houses is the spider's, if they but knew.
build a second one, just in case.
games.why: 29:41: those who take other patrons than God are like the spider and her house, the frailest of all houses.

practice: Think about what you reach for when things wobble: your phone, someone's approval, a bank balance, being busy, being right.

None of these is bad in itself, any more than the spider's silk is, but pick one and ask honestly: if the wind came, would this hold me, and what would? If you pray, you can lean your weight, for this minute, on God.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Ankabut. The spider, whose house, in the Qur'an's picture of leaning on anything other than God, is carefully built, beautiful, and the frailest of all houses. Today's word.
